title: The CLAUDE.md: the rules that make AI animate well
description: A text file with the project's rules is what separates a robotic animation from a carousel with weight and rhythm. Every rule came from a real defect.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: Aura and the agents that show up in this tutorial's carousel.

blocks.text: Have you ever explained the same thing to someone three times and, on the fourth, thought "I should have written this down"? It's the same with AI. Every conversation starts from scratch. If the rule isn't written, it doesn't exist.
In the previous tutorial I showed how AI turns code into video. Now I want to show the file that weighed the most on the result of the Clint carousel: the CLAUDE.md. Shall we?
What the CLAUDE.md is

It's a text file that lives in the project folder. Claude reads it before starting any task there. It works like the house manual: format, rhythm, colors, what's allowed and what isn't. You write it once and it applies to every conversation in that project.
The difference from a regular prompt is that the prompt disappears when the conversation ends. The CLAUDE.md stays. And it grows: every defect that shows up twice becomes a new line.
How I organized mine
I split it into short blocks. Each block answers a question the AI would ask if it could.
What size, how many frames per second, how long each slide lasts, how the loop works.
Which curve to use, how much it can bounce, how often something happens.
Colors, fonts and a list of what's forbidden.
What the company promises and what can't be claimed without a source.
A real interface is a real capture. Anything drawn gets the "conceptual demo" label.
The order of work, with a mandatory stop for me to approve before rendering.

blocks.label: Excerpt from the carousel's CLAUDE.md (condensed)
blocks.text:
## Format
- 1080×1350, 30 fps, one MP4 per slide.
- Slides of 4, 6 or 8 s (120 BPM, one beat every 0.5 s).
- Frame 0 works on its own: title and state readable.
- Seamless loop: the last frame returns to the first.

## Motion
- Nothing linear. Springs with at most one tiny bounce.
- Weight: squash and stretch slightly, preserving volume.
- One event every 2 to 4 s, micro-interactions on the beat.

## Forbidden
- Unsourced numbers, made-up interface pretending to be real.
- Fades on everything, particle explosions, humanoid robots.
Every rule came from a defect

This is the part I like most. After each render, I put together a sheet with one frame per beat and look at it calmly. In the first round of the Clint carousel, five defects showed up. Pick one and see the rule it produced.
How the critique round works, with the real scorecard:
Notice that no rule is generic like "make it pretty". They're all checkable: 36 px, one focus per beat, nothing cropped in any frame. If I can't check it, the AI can't either.
The mandatory stop
The rule that saved me the most time isn't about animation. It's about process: before writing any HTML, the AI shows me the brief, the storyboard and the image inventory, and waits for my ok.

Fixing a line in the storyboard takes a minute. Fixing an already rendered slide takes a lot longer. It was at this stop that I matched the brief with the soundtrack's beat, and the carousel ended up with a single song carrying over from one slide to the next.
How to start yours
Create the CLAUDE.md file in the project folder, with the format and motion blocks. Ten lines are enough.
Ask for just one slide. Look at it frame by frame.
For each defect, write the rule in a way you can check.
Run it again. When the same defect doesn't come back, the rule worked.

blocks.text: In the end, the CLAUDE.md is less about AI and more about direction. It's what an art director would say standing next to your desk, just written down. In the next tutorial I bring it all together: brief, storyboard and the music's beat, slide by slide.
This project's rule structure was inspired by Movez's material and Felipe Borges's skill, adapted for Clint. The links are in the sources.
